title: HealthTrack Monitoring Dashboard: User Interface Design
author: Todd Simonson

paras: The dashboard serves rehab clinicians who check a caseload of home patients between other tasks, so it answers three questions in order: who needs attention first, how the readings compare with that patient's own limits, and what action is required.

sections.heading: Layout
paras: A fixed header sits above three columns that read left to right as triage, assessment, and action (Figure 1): the worklist ranked by most severe active alert; the selected patient's prescription, gauges, and trend charts; and the active alerts with their actions (Table 1).

figure.title: Dashboard During a Critical Heart Rate Alert
figure.note: Synthetic data. Thomas Reed's last two exercise readings exceeded his prescribed 128 bpm ceiling, so his card moved to the top, the readings are drawn as red triangles, and a pop-up was sent to his clinician.

sections.heading: Interaction Flow
paras: After sign-in the top-ranked patient is already selected, so the highest-priority view takes zero clicks, inside the two-click limit of requirement NFR-15. When an alert arrives, the patient's card moves to the top, the alert joins the panel, and a pop-up offers Open patient. The clinician reviews the charts, acknowledges to take ownership and stop escalation, and resolves the alert with a required note. A link in an email or text opens the same patient after sign-in.

sections.heading: Design Decisions
paras: *Meaning never depends on color alone.* Each severity has a color, a glyph, and a word, and abnormal points change both color and shape, following WCAG 2.1 guidance on the use of color (World Wide Web Consortium, 2018). Text contrast is at least 4.6:1, and red is reserved for critical alerts.
*Charts and alerts share one source of limits.* Zone bands and threshold lines are the thresholds the alert engine applies to that patient, so a chart never shows a flagged reading as normal.

*Updates are pushed and drawn incrementally.* WebSocket events arrive in 250 ms batches; new readings are appended in the browser without a server round trip, gauges get partial updates, and a 15-second poll covers a dropped connection. The 7-day view keeps each interval's high, low, and abnormal readings while thinning normal ones.

*Alert fatigue and privacy carry into the screen.* Repeats appear as occurrence counts, each alert shows at most one pop-up, and pop-ups close once the alert is acknowledged. The dashboard server holds the access and refresh tokens; the browser receives only a session cookie and a one-time WebSocket ticket.

references: World Wide Web Consortium. (2018). *Web content accessibility guidelines (WCAG) 2.1*. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/
